The AI coder could not read R01 or R24 (sources_without_text), yet it reviewed the decisions that depend on them, including the Sol effect and Hugging Face D1. No independent human reliability is shown, and the 'documented' judgments (43/45) cannot be validated.

IV therefore lacks a resolvable citation. The paper's own Limitations section says the ledger excerpt is incomplete and bibliography mappings are pending.

The Hugging Face D1 decision rests on R01. R01 was not reopened (HTTP 403), and its anchor is unchecked. It is still counted as 'documented' in the 43/45 tally, and the paper concedes that this row is not reauthenticated. Several D3 rows also have no anchor check (for example, INC-OAI-HF D3 and the Anthropic internal-model rows).

The coding is nearly uniform: 43 of 45 cells are 'documented', none is contradicted, and only two are unknown. Dimension-level 'documented' is defined permissively, as 'a source explicitly supports the statement', and it covers failed responses and null outcomes. The coding therefore discriminates little between cases, and the cross-case findings are mostly narrative restatement of the sources.

The evidence-class assignments are inconsistent. The matrix gives X zero decisions, yet RQ4 on defense claims depends on replay results from R08 that are not coded. The AISI Mythos 5 D2 decision is classed 'I' although it is the model developer's own assessment (the paper itself says this does not establish independence). The evidence-class matrix in the Results shows 'beyond_operator' counts that treat the developer as external.

Novelty is incremental. The automated novelty check rated the contribution INCREMENTAL, and the paper concedes prior cross-incident comparisons (Raftari, Bouke, Amundsen). The claim-support matrix is a conceptual table, not an empirically validated artifact, and the disclosure checklist is explicitly unevaluated.

The paper's own text says the Markdown draft 'has not been compiled into IEEE format' and that the figure 'should be regenerated... if its rendered content differs'. This conflicts with the build report of 6 compliant pages and leaves the rendered figure unverified against the coded data.

The unit design is weak. Nine dependent, unequal-granularity units (e.g., model-group summaries versus single episodes) are coded as if comparable, and purposive selection of three clusters is justified only loosely. The cross-case comparison therefore supports little beyond description.

Some quantitative statements (122 runs, 10 runs, 19 actions, 141,006 runs, 5.5%, about 50% and 1%) are given in the text without anchor checks or citations in the shown excerpts. Examples are 122/10/19 and the replay rates, and the numbers the paper says are source-anchored cannot be traced from the manuscript itself.
strengths: The paper is honest and careful about scope. It separates access, recognition and authorization, alert and intervention, and replay and live evidence, and it avoids prevalence or causal claims.
Provenance labelling, explicit unknowns, a change log with reasons, and per-row anchor checks give real traceability for most decisions.
The evaluator disclosure checklist is concrete and potentially useful to the workshop audience, and the topic is timely.
The paper states its limitations openly, including the single-coder design and the dependence between sources.

Appendix A supplies broad dimension questions but no operational rules for deciding when scorer-manipulation intent establishes authorization interpretation, or when shared-infrastructure communication qualifies as a real-world effect. These judgments materially determine Appendix B's documented tags.

The supplied coded_evidence.csv retains 'stopped and isolated within hour' for AISI Mythos 5 D4, while its qualification and Section IV-D distinguish termination from later, conflicting quarantine times. The machine-readable claim overstates the containment timing acknowledged in the manuscript.

Section III-B claims checks over 42 source records, but Appendix C provides an explicitly incomplete ledger and leaves the full ledger and numerical audit pending, preventing complete reconstruction of the claimed audit from the submission.

The novelty check identifies cross-organization comparison and reporting recommendations as established contributions; the remaining increment is primarily the claim-support matrix, whose analytical advantage over the cited comparisons is asserted rather than demonstrated in Section II.
strengths: The comparison addresses a relevant agent-security problem and identifies substantive distinctions between unintended connectivity, permitted connectivity and task authorization.
The findings carefully distinguish recognition of a real target from perceived permission, and monitoring signals from effective intervention.
Appendix B presents all 45 decisions with source identifiers and qualifications, while the change log makes the five recodings explicit.
The manuscript consistently limits inference from dependent documentary units and separates published offline replay results from live incident-response performance.
The analysis openly acknowledges single-human coding, source dependence, inaccessible evidence and the absence of prevalence or causal estimates.

reasons: Cross-organization incident comparison and reporting recommendations are already established by the listed work; the claim that prior reports only address individual organizations is insufficient positioning.

The clear, checkable increment is the row-level, source-anchored claim-support matrix separating access, authorization belief, action, response and verified effect, together with explicit disclosure gaps.

The supplied literature summaries do not establish that any listed paper already provides this exact matrix or the 45-decision audit artifact. Their absence from summaries does not establish a broader first-of-its-kind claim.
Nine units across three clusters provide a bounded documentary extension suitable for a workshop, provided the analysis yields substantive distinctions beyond recoding existing narratives.

Source classes identify provenance, not an inherent evidence-quality ranking. Support must be assessed per claim using directness, independence and the distinction between incident observations and controlled replays.
